newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Northwest hydropower plants brace for runoff.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Northwest hydropower plants brace for runoff.

text.p: U.S. Northwest hydropower projects will be brought down to minimum flood control levels following the latest runoff forecast from the National Weather Service (NWS), the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers said Monday.
"There is not much revising we can make. Most projects are already aiming for minimum pool targets," said Cindy Henriksen, chief of the Corps' reservoir control center in Portland, Ore.

The NWS Northwest River Forecast Center's latest estimate for January-July runoff at The Dalles dam on the Columbia River in Oregon is 137 percent of average, up from an early-January forecast of 130 percent.
If the forecast is accurate, runoff this year would exceed last year's 132 percent of average by a significant margin.
Runoff at some projects was predicted to be even higher, with the Brownlee reservoir on the Snake River in Idaho forecast to see inflows of 190 percent of normal.
Idaho Power Co had previously been directed to draw Brownlee down to its minimum flood target by the end of April in case storage space is needed to avoid downstream flooding.
But some hydropower reservoirs, such as Hungry Horse in Montana, which can be taken taken down another five feet, will have their targets lowered, Henriksen noted.
The Libby reservoir, also in Montana, would have its flood control level reduced, while the Grand Coulee project in Washington was already set to come down to within three feet of minimum, she said.
According to Corps of Engineers statistics, most federal hydropower projects in the Northwest were running the extra water through power turbines, with only minimal amounts being spilled.
